scope: Primary sources only. No repository edits. No evidence found for a guaranteed daily 3-stock, +10% within 5 sessions, no-loss strategy.

sources.title: Momentum Crashes
sources.market_horizon: U.S. common stocks 1927–2013; prior 12-to-2-month returns, monthly rebalanced decile portfolios; international/other asset-class replication.
sources.costs: Principal cumulative-return illustration explicitly assumes no transaction costs.
sources.finding: Momentum long-short portfolios suffer persistent crashes, especially high-volatility rebounds after market declines; much of this is the short loser portfolio rising sharply. Dynamic strategy exposure helps in the paper's experiments.
sources.quality: Original authors, NBER full-text working paper; later peer-reviewed JFE publication. Disclosed AQR relationship.
sources.application: Stress-state and tail-risk awareness, not evidence that a long-only daily 3-stock crash-rebound basket is safe. Do not transplant long-short crash results as a proven long-only reject rule.

sources.title: Momentum Has Its Moments
sources.market_horizon: Cross-sectional equity momentum portfolios; multi-month formation, risk-managed portfolio leverage. Fetched author abstract, not final full text.
sources.costs: Fetched abstract does not establish net retail KR execution returns.
sources.finding: Authors find momentum risk is time-varying and predictable, and scaling its exposure materially reduces historical crash risk.
sources.quality: Author SSRN page identifies JFE 116(1):111–120; claims here limited to abstract.
sources.application: Risk scaling is a position/exposure decision. This newsletter chooses names, so it cannot claim to implement the paper solely by changing ATR rank.

sources.title: Volatility-Managed Portfolios
sources.market_horizon: Monthly U.S. equity factors and currency carry; monthly returns scaled by inverse previous-month realized variance.
sources.costs: Paper discusses realistic costs and tight leverage constraints; this is not a KR retail 5-day stock-selection estimate.
sources.finding: Taking less portfolio risk after high realized volatility improves risk-adjusted results in studied factors; volatility and expected return do not rise proportionately.
sources.quality: Original published Journal of Finance paper on author's site; full-text extraction read.
sources.application: High volatility alone is not a reward signal. Explicitly distinct from cross-sectional low-volatility name selection and from +10% hit classification.

sources.title: On the Performance of Volatility-Managed Portfolios
sources.authors: Scott Cederburg; Michael S. O'Doherty; Feifei Wang; Xuemin (Sterling) Yan
sources.market_horizon: 103 equity strategies; real-time out-of-sample combinations of managed/unmanaged portfolios.
sources.costs: Main negative result concerns implementability and unstable estimated weights, not a promised net trading result.
sources.finding: Managed portfolios do not systematically outperform direct counterparts. Feasible out-of-sample combinations generally have lower Sharpe/utility; instability in spanning regressions explains degradation. Some momentum/ROE/BAB results remain positive.
sources.quality: Peer-reviewed JFE 138:95–117; final paper on coauthor university site; explicit contrary replication evidence.
sources.application: Do not sell risk management as universally performance-improving. Test the exact feasible selector with past-only parameters and the actual holding horizon.

sources.title: Maxing Out: Stocks as Lotteries and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
sources.authors: Turan G. Bali; Nusret Cakici; Robert F. Whitelaw
sources.market_horizon: U.S. equities July 1962–December 2005; prior-month maximum daily return, next-month portfolio returns.
sources.costs: Cross-sectional return evidence; not a net 5-day retail execution strategy.
sources.finding: Higher past-month maximum daily returns predict lower average subsequent returns after multiple controls. Lottery-like upside appeal can coexist with poor expected return.
sources.quality: Original NBER full text; later JFE 99(2):427–446. Distinct from claiming ATR is itself MAX.
sources.application: Evaluate recent extreme spikes and distress separately from upside touch probability. Never use high ATR or one large prior up-day as sufficient evidence of positive expected return.

sources.title: Benchmarks as Limits to Arbitrage: Understanding the Low-Volatility Anomaly
sources.authors: Malcolm Baker; Brendan Bradley; Jeffrey Wurgler
sources.market_horizon: U.S. CRSP January 1968–December 2008; monthly quintile sorts on up to 60 months of volatility/beta; top-1,000-stock robustness.
sources.costs: Displayed portfolios explicitly exclude transaction costs; yearly rebalancing robustness discussed.
sources.finding: Low-volatility/low-beta diversified portfolios historically outperform high-risk counterparts, with benchmarking constraints offered as an explanation.
sources.quality: Published Financial Analysts Journal paper on coauthor university site; author asset-manager affiliations disclosed.
sources.application: Useful warning against maximizing volatility, but no evidence for picking the 3 minimum-ATR names to gain 10% within 5 sessions; long-horizon portfolio evidence differs.

sources.title: A Taxonomy of Anomalies and Their Trading Costs
sources.market_horizon: U.S. cross-sectional anomaly portfolios, varied trading frequencies/turnover.
sources.costs: Directly models costs and mitigation. Few high-turnover strategies remain significant; buy/hold spread reduces unnecessary turnover.
sources.finding: Transaction costs reduce all studied strategies' profit and significance. Equal weighting often worsens net results because it loads on expensive-to-trade names.
sources.quality: Original NBER full text; published RFS 29(1):104–147. Relevant authors' industry ties disclosed.
sources.application: Retain measurable liquidity requirements and evaluate net returns. A daily new 3-stock product is not economically equivalent to low-turnover factor portfolios; don't infer no-cost touch as user gain.

sources.title: Trading Costs
sources.authors: Andrea Frazzini; Ronen Israel; Tobias J. Moskowitz
sources.market_horizon: 1.7 trillion USD of real institutional executions, 21 developed equity markets, 19 years.
sources.costs: Explicit realized costs/price impact across trade type, size, stock, time and exchange; abstract reports costs lower than older models.
sources.finding: Cost estimates should reflect actual execution and capacity; optimized institutional trading can be materially cheaper than generic estimates.
sources.quality: Original author working paper based on proprietary practitioner execution data; single-manager selection limits generalization; abstract fetched.
sources.application: Do not assign institutional optimized fills to retail newsletter users. Use transparent spread/slippage/tax assumptions and sensitivity; avoid arbitrary universal slippage claims.

sources.title: What You See Is Not What You Get: The Costs of Trading Market Anomalies
sources.authors: Andrew J. Patton; Brian M. Weller
sources.market_horizon: U.S. mutual-fund implementations of value/momentum exposures versus on-paper factor returns.
sources.costs: Estimates all-in implementation costs including investability constraints rather than only quoted commissions.
sources.finding: Typical mutual funds in their sample realize low value returns and no momentum returns after implementation costs; single skilled manager costs may not generalize.
sources.quality: Peer-reviewed JFE 137:515–549 full text on coauthor university site; useful counterweight to single-manager execution studies.
sources.application: Evaluate recommendation outcomes from an executable user entry and actual exit definition. A high touched 10% before a deep drawdown is not the same as realized profit.

sources.title: When Do Stop-Loss Rules Stop Losses?
sources.authors: Kathryn M. Kaminski; Andrew W. Lo
sources.market_horizon: Published version: daily index-futures data and buy-and-hold strategies; benefits in certain longer sampling intervals.
sources.costs: Final institutional abstract does not establish retail-stock cost-adjusted 5-day exits. Earlier 2007/2010 drafts use different monthly stock/bond samples and must not be conflated.
sources.finding: Stop-loss value is conditional on the price process and implementation; certain rules can reduce volatility and raise expected returns, rather than stopping all losses.
sources.quality: MIT repository record for final Journal of Financial Markets 18:234–254 original manuscript. Earlier author SSRN draft separately read.
sources.application: A stop is an execution rule, not a selection guarantee. Don't add hypothetical stops to recommendation success unless user execution is modeled; daily OHLC cannot resolve same-day target/stop order.

sources.title: Stop Orders in Select Futures Markets
sources.market_horizon: Audit-trail orders/trades in E-mini S&P 500, 10-year Treasury-note and WTI futures, 2014–2016.
sources.costs: Observes placement/execution, slippage and exchange protection levels; not KR-stock stop execution.
sources.finding: Stop-order trades cluster with volatility; stop-market slippage can be significant and behavior differs by participants/products.
sources.quality: Primary CFTC Office of Chief Economist staff paper using regulatory order data, not a Commission guarantee or equity study.
sources.application: Even an actual stop price is not a guaranteed fill price. Evaluate gap/illiquidity losses; never assert 'loss impossible' because a stop level was assigned.

sources.title: Replicating Anomalies
sources.authors: Kewei Hou; Chen Xue; Lu Zhang
sources.market_horizon: Large U.S. anomaly replication library, 452 variables; decile portfolios with NYSE breakpoints/value weighting.
sources.costs: Microcap/investability sensitivity and multiple testing; not all-in execution validation of every strategy.
sources.finding: 65% fail a single-test significance threshold after microcap mitigation; 82% fail the multiple-test threshold. Replicated effects are often smaller than originally reported.
sources.quality: Final peer-reviewed RFS 33:2019–2133 full text on authors' research site. Final counts differ from earlier NBER draft (447 variables), so do not mix versions.
sources.application: Treat tiny/illiquid-stock gains and repeated parameter searches skeptically. A famous factor name is not enough to validate this exact KR/5-day/3-name policy.

sources.title: …and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
sources.authors: Campbell R. Harvey; Yan Liu; Heqing Zhu
sources.market_horizon: Asset-pricing factor literature and multiple-testing framework, not a security-selection portfolio.
sources.finding: Searching many related factors and publication selection raises the evidence hurdle beyond an isolated conventional t-test.
sources.quality: Original author SSRN manuscript; published RFS 29(1):5–68. Author profile now Caroline Zhu; publication author Heqing Zhu.
sources.application: Keep the number of tried strategy variants visible in analysis. Reusing the existing 180 days cannot be re-labelled untouched out-of-sample after choosing a winner on it.

sources.title: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting
sources.authors: David H. Bailey; Jonathan Borwein; Marcos López de Prado; Qiji Jim Zhu
sources.market_horizon: Investment-backtest selection methodology; combinatorially symmetric cross-validation.
sources.finding: Holdout results can be unreliable after many strategy configurations are selected; proposes quantifying probability of backtest overfitting.
sources.quality: Original author manuscript on SSRN; fetched version dated February 27, 2015, listed forthcoming in Journal of Computational Finance.
sources.application: Do not repeatedly tune against the same validation data and declare success. Chronological evaluation with overlapping 5-day labels kept out of training is an engineering requirement; this citation does not validate any particular threshold.

implementation: Keep UI and existing overall-score formula unchanged. If a minimum overall score is required, apply it to the actual score before selection; do not inflate or relabel it as probability.
Separate upside-touch target from realized user outcome. Compare 5-day net close return, probability of net loss and downside excursion alongside touch; +10% intraday can coexist with loss.

Treat extreme ATR and recent lottery-like spikes as risk information rather than automatically positive ranking inputs. Any cutoffs must be justified against this market/horizon, not copied from factor papers.
Portfolio volatility scaling, stops, and take-profit orders are execution or sizing rules. A recommendation-only product does not implement them merely by printing names.

Retain freshness and liquidity checks. Use executable next-session entry, conservative cost/slippage assumptions, and explicit handling of both target and stop hit on one daily bar if simulating exits.

Use past-only train/tune dates with label horizon separation; already-reused history is research evaluation, not untouched OOS. Avoid a large hyperparameter sweep solely to obtain attractive backtest numbers.

Always returning exactly 3 while imposing a genuine high-score floor can be infeasible on some days. Do not silently lower the floor or substitute low-quality candidates; surface this product constraint internally for parent resolution.
None of these references justify guaranteeing that every user avoids losses or earns +10%. Three concentrated long positions retain stock, market, execution, and gap risk.
